top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: During those energized periods, have you ever needed to be hospitalized, or done anything so risky or out of character that it caused major problems?
turns.patient_response:
Hospitalized? Oh, no, no. Never anything like that. Even when I'm running on that really high, intense energy, I've never done anything wild or dangerous, you know? I haven't gambled away my savings or driven a hundred miles an hour down the highway or done anything that would blow up my life. It’s never reached that level of chaos where someone needed to step in and take me to a hospital. 

But if you're asking if all of this has caused problems... well, yes, but in a much more mundane, frustrating way. My work has stayed intact overall—I haven't been fired, and the executives still rely on me—but I’ve definitely noticed a slip. Like I mentioned earlier with that flight mistake, I’ve been missing calendar details. And for an executive assistant, the calendar is the holy grail. I find myself having to double-check tasks that used to be completely automatic for me. I used to be able to look at a multi-city travel itinerary and instantly know if a layover was too short, just by instinct. Now? I’m staring at the screen, tracing the times with my finger, checking it two or three times because I just don't trust my own brain to catch the mistakes on the first pass anymore. It’s exhausting to have to manually process things that used to just flow naturally.

And because of that, because I'm spending so much mental energy just trying to keep the plates spinning at work and making sure I don't drop the ball, I’ve really had to pull back from the rest of my life. I haven't been doing my photography outings at all lately. I used to love packing up my gear, driving out to the state park before dawn, and just waiting for the perfect light... but I just don't go anymore. I’ve stepped back from mentoring the junior administrative staff, too. I used to take them out for coffee, review their workflows, give them advice on how to handle difficult personalities. But I just don’t feel as present or reliable these days. How can I sit there and confidently tell a twenty-three-year-old how to manage a CEO's life when I'm secretly second-guessing my own basic calendar invites? I just don't feel like I have it in me to be the rock they need right now. So, no, no major disasters or hospital stays, just... a lot of stepping back and double-checking to make sure the wheels don't completely fall off.

turns.doctor_question: During those energized periods, do other people ever tell you that you seem unusually talkative or hard to interrupt?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. Yes. And it’s funny you ask that, because my wife is usually the very first person to bring it up. She’ll be sitting at the kitchen island, just trying to have her morning coffee, and I will just be going a mile a minute. And it’s not just her, either, it’s my coworkers at the office, too. They all tell me that I talk so incredibly fast during those stretches that they literally cannot get a single word in edgewise. 

Because, you see, my brain is just making all these connections, and I feel like I have to get it all out right that second. So I’ll start off talking to them about something administrative, like, say, overhauling the employee medical forms—which, let me tell you, is a massive undertaking because the compliance regulations change every single year and nobody ever wants to read the fine print—but before they can even process what I’m saying about the medical forms, I’ve already jumped completely over to the upcoming work deadlines. And then, without even taking a breath, I’m suddenly pitching them on all these new mentoring ideas I have for the junior administrative team. 

To me, in the moment, it all makes perfect sense. It’s all connected, it’s all part of the same ecosystem of keeping the company running smoothly. But they tell me it’s just this overwhelming wall of sound. My wife actually has to hold her hand up like a stop sign sometimes just to break my momentum. She tells me I just jump from the medical forms to the work deadlines to the mentoring ideas so fast that she gets dizzy trying to follow the thread. And I don’t even realize I’m doing it until someone physically stops me, because I just have so much energy and so many ideas that I feel like if I don't say them all out loud right then and there, I'll burst. So, yes, unusually talkative is probably an understatement.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient explicitly states that they talk excessively, noting that 'unusually talkative is probably an understatement.'
symptom_reasoning.S037: The patient describes talking 'so incredibly fast' that others 'cannot get a single word in edgewise' and feeling a pressure to speak before they 'burst.'
symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient describes a flight of ideas and racing thoughts, stating their brain is 'making all these connections' and they rapidly jump between multiple unrelated topics.

turns.doctor_question: During those energized periods, do you feel unusually confident or like you have special abilities compared with usual?
turns.patient_response:
Well, confidence is... I mean, yes, absolutely, but "confident" almost feels like too small a word for it. It goes way beyond just feeling good about myself or my work. When I get into one of those really high-energy gears, it’s like... it’s like I suddenly have this crystal-clear vision that nobody else possesses. I don't just feel capable; I feel entirely indispensable. Like I am the absolute linchpin holding everything together. 

I’ll look at all the moving parts in my life, and I’ll feel like I’m the only one who can straighten out the doctors, the family, and the office. All of it. At the exact same time. I'll be coordinating with medical offices for my executives—which, let me tell you, is usually a complete nightmare trying to get specialists to align with a corporate travel schedule—and I'm dealing with my own family's affairs, and I'm running the entire administrative floor, and I just think, "Everyone else is moving in slow motion and I am the only one who actually knows how to fix this." 

And it gets to the point where I start believing my system is better than anyone else’s judgment. Period. Like, normally, I'm very collaborative. I'll take feedback, I'll listen to the junior staff. But during these stretches? If someone suggests a different way to route an itinerary or my wife wants to handle a household issue differently, I just completely dismiss them. I look at them and think, "You don't see the big picture here. You don't get it." Because my system—the way I've cross-referenced the calendars, the way I've mapped out the timelines—feels completely flawless to me. I feel like I have this special ability to just engineer reality better than anyone else, and if they would all just step back and let me dictate how things should run, everything would be absolutely perfect. So, yes, I get incredibly confident. I just feel like I'm operating on a completely different, superior frequency than the rest of the world.

symptom_reasoning.S035: The patient explicitly confirms feeling unusually confident, believing they have a 'crystal-clear vision nobody else possesses,' and feeling they operate on a 'superior frequency' with a 'special ability to engineer reality.'
symptom_reasoning.S040: The patient describes taking on multiple tasks simultaneously across work and personal life (coordinating with medical offices, dealing with family affairs, running the administrative floor) during these high-energy periods.

turns.doctor_question: Have these high-energy periods ever caused you to need much less sleep without feeling tired the next day?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. Sleep just completely goes out the window during those times. It’s actually one of the most noticeable things, now that I think about it. Normally, I am someone who needs a solid seven or eight hours, or I’m just dragging the next day, relying on espresso to get me through the afternoon slump. But when I get into one of those high-energy gears? It’s a totally different story. 

There have been nights—many nights, actually, during those stretches—when I will finally force myself into bed at maybe midnight, and then, boom, my eyes pop open and it's 2:30 or 3:00 AM. I’ll sleep maybe two or three hours, tops. And the crazy thing is, I don't wake up groggy. I wake up before dawn, and I feel completely wired, just buzzing with energy. I don't feel tired at all. Instead of tossing and turning or trying to force myself back to sleep like a normal person would, I just get right up. I'll make a pot of coffee in the dark, open up my laptop, and I am instantly ready to answer emails or start updating the executive appointment lists. 

And you have to understand, those appointment lists are incredibly tedious to manage during normal business hours because you're constantly fighting with other assistants for time slots and dealing with last-minute cancellations. But at 3:30 in the morning? It’s perfectly quiet. Nobody is pinging me on the company messaging app. So I’m just sitting there in the pitch black, color-coding calendar blocks, matching up time zones for international conference calls, just blasting through my inbox and organizing everything for the next three weeks. 

My wife will come out to the kitchen at 5:30 to get a glass of water, and she’ll just stare at me because I’ve already been working at a dead sprint for two hours. She'll ask if I slept at all, and I'll tell her, honestly, I feel like I slept for ten hours. My body just somehow decides that two or three hours is more than enough, and my brain is just screaming at me to get ahead of the day before the sun even comes up. So, yes, drastically less sleep, but zero fatigue the next day. None whatsoever. I just keep going and going.

symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient describes feeling completely wired, buzzing with energy, and working at a dead sprint.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient explicitly states they sleep only two or three hours but wake up feeling like they slept for ten hours with zero fatigue.

turns.doctor_question: Did this period of feeling flat and heavy start only after the family situation became stressful, or had you already been feeling this way before that?
turns.patient_response:
Well, to answer your question, it was definitely after. Definitely after. Because if I look back on the timeline, this whole... this heavy, just completely flat feeling where I just feel weighed down by everything? It’s been going on for about a year and three months now. Give or take a couple of weeks, but right around a year and three months. 

And I can pinpoint it because it started exactly after my family member’s health took a turn and their behavior started changing so drastically. You see, when that happened, somebody had to step in and take over the logistics, and naturally, because of what I do for a living, that fell to me. I took on all the extra coordination. And coordinating medical care for a relative, let me tell you, is a full-time job on its own. It is completely different from managing a corporate office. You're dealing with different specialists who refuse to talk to each other, you're trying to manage the pharmacy refills, you're navigating these sudden behavioral changes that you just aren't prepared for... and I was trying to juggle all of that on top of my actual job at the office. 

So I was coordinating their appointments, coordinating their daily needs, just constantly organizing and fixing things for them because nobody else in the family has the administrative skillset to handle it properly. And it was only after I took all of that on, after the reality of their health and behavior changes really hit and I became the central point of contact for everything, that this flat feeling started. Before that, I wasn't feeling this way at all, I was managing just fine. But for the last fifteen months, ever since I took on that coordination, it's just been this constant, heavy feeling that I can't seem to shake.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes a persistent 'heavy, just completely flat feeling' where they feel 'weighed down by everything.'
symptom_reasoning.S081: The patient explicitly links the onset of their emotional symptoms (the flat, heavy feeling) to the identifiable stressor of taking on the intense coordination of a family member's medical care.

turns.doctor_question: Have there ever been times when you felt so unusually energized or irritable that other people said you were not yourself, and it caused clear problems at work, home, or with relationships?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it’s a mix of both, really, and it can flip on a dime, which is what catches people off guard. Because I will have these stretches—like I was mentioning earlier with the energy and the system I build—where I just feel unusually upbeat. I mean, I’m practically humming as I walk down the hall. I feel like everything is just clicking perfectly into place. The executives’ schedules are a well-oiled machine, the travel itineraries are flawless, the household is running smoothly, and I’m just riding this incredible wave of feeling fantastic and capable. 

But then... and this is where it gets tricky, and where people definitely notice something is off with my personality... because I’m so wired and everything is so "perfect" in my head, if there is even a tiny, microscopic change? I can become incredibly sharp with people. I mean, snapping at them in a way that honestly surprises even me. 

Like, say, one of the junior VP’s assistants decides they need to move a 2:00 PM strategy meeting to 2:15 PM. Normally? That is standard office procedure. No big deal, I drag and drop the calendar block, I send an update, we move on. But during these stretches where I'm so elevated? I will just lay into them. I get so intensely irritable because they don't see the domino effect. I'll snap and tell them that if they move that to 2:15, then the 3:00 PM conference call with London gets pushed, and then the car service to the airport is off schedule, and how could they be so careless? I'll send these really curt, almost aggressive emails that are completely out of character for me. 

And it happens at home, too. My wife might just ask to push our dinner plans back by half an hour because she's running late, and I will just bite her head off. She’s actually had to stop me in the middle of the kitchen and say, "Who are you right now? Why are you acting like this over a dinner reservation?" And at the office, I've had coworkers actively avoid my desk because I get so visibly agitated over these minor scheduling tweaks. So it definitely causes friction, because one minute I’m the most upbeat guy on the administrative floor, completely on top of the world, and the next, I’m lashing out over a fifteen-minute calendar shift.

symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient describes distinct periods of feeling 'unusually upbeat' and 'wired' that can quickly flip into intense irritability, causing friction at work and home.
symptom_reasoning.S060: The patient admits to having low frustration tolerance during these periods, snapping and reacting sharply to minor stimuli like a 15-minute schedule change.
